41	\label{sec:learned_compression}
42	
43	If hard pruning fails on SmolVLA because every token is indispensable, why does learned compression with cross-attention pooling succeed? The answer lies in the distinction between deletion and aggregation. Hard pruning applies a binary mask: selected tokens are kept verbatim, and the rest are discarded with their information permanently lost. Cross-attention pooling operates differently. A set of $M$ learned query vectors attends over all 128 source tokens through standard cross-attention, and each query computes a weighted sum across the full token set. Even when the output is compressed to $M = 32$ (a 75\% reduction in token count), every original token contributes to the compressed representation through its attention weight. No information is deleted; it is redistributed into fewer, higher-capacity vectors.

\paragraph{The inverted-U shape.}
The non-monotonic relationship between $M$ and performance reveals that compression is not merely tolerated but actively beneficial. At $M = 96$ (25\% compression), the bottleneck is too wide: the compressor passes most information through without forcing selective aggregation, and performance drops to 52.6\%. At $M = 16$ (87.5\% compression), the bottleneck is too narrow: 16 queries cannot preserve sufficient spatial information from 128 source tokens, and performance drops to 55.8\%. The sweet spot at $M \in \{32, 64\}$ balances information preservation against the regularization benefit of the bottleneck. Notably, $M = 32$ achieves peak performance at the highest compression ratio among all tested configurations, making it the optimal choice for deployment: maximum token reduction with no performance penalty relative to lighter compression. Per-task distributions differ between $M = 32$ and $M = 64$ (Table~\ref{tab:smart_compress_pertask}, Appendix~\ref{app:per_task}), with differences up to 26 percentage points on individual tasks despite identical aggregate SR.

\paragraph{Compression as a cost-free deployment benefit.}
The flat performance profile across $M \in \{32, 64, 128\}$ (59.8\%--61.6\%) reveals that reducing token count from 128 to 32 incurs no measurable performance penalty. Compression is therefore a pure deployment benefit: 75\% KV-cache reduction and modest latency improvement (Section~\ref{sec:cost_benefit}) without trading off task performance. $M = 32$ is the optimal deployment configuration because it combines peak SR with maximum token reduction. Only at $M = 16$ does information loss from extreme compression (87.5\%) begin to degrade performance, though the 55.8\% SR remains well above baseline. Per-task distributions differ between configurations (Table~\ref{tab:smart_compress_pertask}, Appendix~\ref{app:per_task}), with differences up to 26 percentage points on individual tasks despite similar aggregate SR.
